scope: Asset-pricing/statistical-learning theory of when a high-dimensional ridge-on-random-features SDF estimator (DKKM) beats low-dimensional sorted-factor (FF) or cross-sectional-regression (FM) estimators; verification against the actual BOP code (config.py, utils_factors/dkkm_functions.py, utils_factors/fama_functions.py, utils/evaluate_sdfs.py, utils_bgn|kp14|gs21/sdf_compute_*.py), against the realised BOP results (bop-analyze-remote/all_results.pdf, MLP Analyze correlations.csv), and against the published real-data benchmark (Didisheim-Ke-Kelly-Malamud, "APT or AIPT", NBER w33012; Kelly-Malamud-Zhou JF 2024). Includes three original numerical experiments I ran: (1) the eigenvalue spectrum / effective rank of the exact RFF feature map as configured in config.py; (2) an oracle-span calculation of the maximum attainable conditional Sharpe inside the linear-char span vs the RFF span under alternative DGPs; (3) the same with T=360 estimation noise added. Scripts in /private/tmp/claude-503/-Users-sjpruitt-GitHub-bop-run-upload/c19e08d3-1736-4cbf-9117-7e2b1e92760e/scratchpad/{rff2.py,span2.py,est3.py,effrank.py}.

findings.claim: The Sharpe metric used here is EXACTLY the true-covariance cosine between the estimated weight vector and the true MVE weight, scaled by the true maximum conditional Sharpe: SR_t(w) = SR*_t · cos_{Sigma_t}(w, w*_t), where w*_t = Sigma_t^{-1} rp_t and SR*_t = sqrt(rp' Sigma^{-1} rp) = the stored `max_sr`. It is scale-invariant in w, so nothing about leverage or SDF calibration is being measured, and every method's score is bounded above by SR*_t.
findings.evidence: evaluate_sdfs.py lines 183-184 compute stdev = sqrt(w' cond_var w) and mean = w' rp; create_slides_tables.py line 36 forms sharpe = mean/stdev and averages over months. Algebra: w'mu = w' Sigma Sigma^{-1} mu = w' Sigma w*, so w'mu / sqrt(w'Sigma w) = [w'Sigma w* / (sqrt(w'Sigma w) sqrt(w*'Sigma w*))] * sqrt(mu'Sigma^{-1}mu). This is an identity, not an approximation. Consequence: the ONLY way any method improves is by rotating w toward w* in the Sigma metric — variance reduction that does not change direction is invisible, and negative cosines produce the negative KP14 Sharpes (-2.6 FF, -5.3 FM).

findings.claim: THE BINDING BLOCKER: under exact K-factor pricing (mu = B lambda, Sigma = B Omega B' + D) with N=1000 and K small, the maximum attainable conditional Sharpe is achieved to within ~0.2% by ANY well-diversified portfolio with the right factor exposure. There is essentially nothing for ANY basis — linear, quadratic, or 3600-dimensional — to add. All three structural models are frictionless rational-expectations economies with K=1 (GS21) or K=2 (BGN, KP14) priced aggregate shocks and no pricing wedge, so they sit exactly in this regime.
findings.evidence: Direct computation (span2.py). With beta=1+2*x1, sigma_f=5%/mo, lambda=0.5%/mo, N=1000: SR*=0.0999, equal-weight market=0.0998, linear-char span (6 portfolios)=0.0999, quadratic (21)=0.0999, RFF-as-configured=0.0994. Adding extreme idiosyncratic-variance dispersion (d proportional to exp(6*x2), a 20x spread in variance) changes nothing: SR*=0.1000, lin=0.1000, RFF=0.0999. The relative shortfall of a naive diversified portfolio is 1/(2 sigma_f^2 beta'D^{-1}beta) ~ (1/2N)(sigma_e^2/sigma_f^2): measured 1.81% at N=100, 0.186% at N=1000, 0.019% at N=10000. Structural confirmation: sdf_compute_gs21.py integrates over exactly one aggregate state x (line 92, x = rho_x*x_prev + sigma_x*nodes); z is per-firm. sdf_compute_bgn.py has one log-SDF shock plus the correlated rate shock. So Sigma_t = (rank 1 or 2) + diagonal by construction and mu is the covariance with the SDF by construction — there is no non-risk component of expected return.

findings.claim: DKKM's own Theorem 3 gives the exact criterion, and it is a criterion on the EFFECTIVE RANK of E[F_t F_t'] (participation ratio (tr M)^2 / tr(M^2)). They calibrate eigenvalues eta_p = p^{-alpha}: alpha=0.5 (EffRank ~ 500) reproduces the empirical virtue of complexity; alpha=2.0 (EffRank ~ 2.5) is their 'APT calibration' in which complexity produces NO gain and actually HURTS at light shrinkage, with peak performance at c << 1. The BOP results are a textbook reproduction of the APT calibration.
findings.evidence: NBER w33012, section 4.6.3: 'When eigenvalues are concentrated, complexity has a small net effect on SDF Sharpe, and can potentially reduce it. However, when the eigenvalue distribution is relatively flat, the Sharpe ratio tends to increase with complexity.' Section 4.7.2: 'there are no benefits to complexity when the eigenvalue distribution is highly concentrated. When the ridge penalty is small (e.g. z <= 1e-5), high-complexity models have lower Sharpe ratios and larger pricing errors than models with complexity near zero.' Match to BOP: GS21 at alpha=0 goes 0.4979 (P=6) -> 0.4761 (36) -> 0.0337 (360) -> 0.1767 (3600); BGN at alpha=0 goes 0.2442 -> 0.2184 -> 0.0060 -> 0.0866; HJD at alpha=0, P=360 explodes to 18.52 (BGN) and 23.57 (GS21). Peak Sharpe is reached at heavy shrinkage and is flat in P. That is Figure 14 of the AIPT paper, not Figure 2.

findings.claim: MEASURED: the RFF feature map exactly as configured in config.py has an effective rank of only 16.5 (5 chars) / 20.7 (6 chars), i.e. the 3600 'factors' are a ~17-dimensional object. Nominal c = P/T = 3600/360 = 10; effective c ~ 0.046. The estimator is operating deep in the classical low-dimensional regime, so the P/T asymptotics that generate the virtue of complexity never engage.
findings.evidence: rff2.py / effrank.py, using the exact code path of dkkm_functions.rff (rank-standardize chars to [-0.5,0.5], W = gamma*N(0,1) with gamma drawn per row from np.arange(0.5,1.1,0.1), features [sin(Wx); cos(Wx)], then rank-standardize the features again). N=1000, 1800 directions (P=3600). Participation-ratio effective rank of the cross-sectional feature second moment: L=5 -> 16.50; L=6 -> 20.71; L=10 -> 38.51; L=20 -> 98.25; L=50 -> 432.4; L=130 -> 773.5. Top-21 PCs carry 90.1% of feature variance at L=5. Fitting this to DKKM's eta_p = p^{-alpha} over P=3600 gives alpha ~ 1.22 for the BOP configuration, versus their AIPT alpha=0.5 and APT alpha=2.0.

findings.claim: MEASURED: with only 5 rank-standardized characteristics the random index w'x has sd = 0.53 (99th pctile |z| = 1.55), so sin/cos are operating on their near-linear/near-quadratic range. The average RFF feature has R^2 = 0.860 against a degree-2 polynomial in the 5 chars; going to degree 3 adds only 0.018. The 3600-feature basis is, to 86% of its variance, quadratic in 5 characteristics — barely richer than Fama-MacBeth plus interactions.
findings.evidence: rff2.py Part A. sd(w'x) = gamma*sqrt(L/12) so with gamma<=1.0 and L=5 the ceiling is 0.645. Mean feature R^2 on linear (dim 6) = 0.489, on quadratic (dim 21) = 0.860, on cubic (dim 56) = 0.878. Same measurement with L=130 gives sd(z)=2.72 and mean R^2 on linear = 0.169. Note that DKKM use the IDENTICAL gamma grid [0.5,...,1.0] and the identical [-0.5,0.5] rank-standardization (w33012 footnote 12 and section 2.5) — the bandwidth is not miscalibrated relative to the published method; it is the input dimension L that differs (130 vs 5).

findings.claim: CRITICAL COUNTEREXAMPLE that rules out 'too few characteristics' as the fundamental cause: DKKM run their complex model on exactly the same five characteristics BOP use (size, value, investment, profitability, momentum) and the OOS tangency Sharpe still goes from 0.74 (FF6) to 1.93-2.50, i.e. a 2.6-3.4x gain. Same 5 chars, same gamma grid, same T=360, same rank-standardization. So the missing ingredient is in the DATA GENERATING PROCESS, not in the characteristic count or the RFF hyperparameters.
findings.evidence: NBER w33012 section 3.3: 'The original formulation of the FF6 model has an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of 0.74, while its high complexity version ranges from 1.93 to 2.50 depending on the degree of shrinkage. All benchmarks show the same pattern... the out-of-sample performance of the benchmarks improves by a factor of 1.4 to 3.6.' They use P=360,000 (c=1000) for that result. In real data the true SDF weight is a strongly nonlinear function of those five characteristics; in BGN/KP14/GS21 it is not (or the nonlinear part is unlearnable).

findings.claim: ORACLE SPAN EXPERIMENT: the RFF span buys nothing over the linear-char span unless expected returns contain a component NOT proportional to the covariance loadings ('alpha'). Once such a component exists, the gains are large, and they are multiplied by characteristic-linked idiosyncratic variance. Heteroskedastic D is a MULTIPLIER on an unspanned premium, never a standalone source of gain.
findings.evidence: span2.py, population (no estimation) maximum Sharpe attainable inside each span, N=1000. (a) exact factor pricing: SR*=0.100, lin=0.100, RFFcfg=0.0994 -> ratio RFF/lin = 0.994-0.999. (b) linear alpha 0.003*x3, homogeneous d: SR*=0.2915, lin=0.2915, RFF=0.2913 -> ratio 1.00 (linear alpha is fully in the FM span). (c) same linear alpha with d proportional to exp(6*x2): SR*=0.930, lin=0.290, quad=0.658, RFFcfg=0.820 -> RFF/lin = 1.91; lin/SR* collapses to 0.31. This is the H2 ratio-nonlinearity channel, and it works ONLY in the presence of alpha. (d) nonlinear/interactive alpha, homogeneous d: SR*=0.954, lin=0.107, quad=0.689, RFFcfg=0.921 -> RFF/lin = 8.6. (e) nonlinear alpha + heteroskedastic d: SR*=3.16, lin=0.110, RFFcfg=2.33 -> RFF/lin = 21.

findings.claim: In the baseline runs NO method recovers anything at all: the cross-sectional correlation between each method's stock weight and the true SDF weight is 0.0000-0.006 in absolute value for FF, FM and DKKM in all three models. All three estimators are, at the individual-stock level, noise. A DKKM-vs-FF gap cannot be detected between three noise vectors.
findings.evidence: MLP Analyze/Full run/results/correlations.csv: bgn fm 0.0025, ff 0.0000099, dkkm 0.0010; gs21 fm 0.0058, ff 0.0036, dkkm 0.0045; kp14 fm -0.0080, ff -0.0053, dkkm -0.0069. sd across months is ~0.032-0.037, i.e. all these are within one cross-month standard deviation of zero. Raising SNR is therefore necessary; but note it moves DKKM only 4% above FF, so it is not sufficient.

findings.claim: The BOP estimator machinery is behaving exactly as random matrix theory predicts, which rules out an implementation bug as the explanation. The c=1 double-descent singularity is visible with textbook precision at P=360, T=360, alpha=0.
findings.evidence: all_results.pdf Table 3 (BGN): HJD at alpha=0 is 0.2152 (P=6), 0.2901 (36), 18.5220 (360), 0.9278 (3600). Table 9 (GS21): 0.3358, 0.3898, 23.5690, 0.9973. The spike is exactly at P=T=360 and disappears with any shrinkage. dkkm_functions.ridge_regr correctly switches to the kernel trick at p_>=t_ (lines 165-178) and the penalty is 360*z with z = nfeatures*alpha supplied by estimate_sdf_dkkm.py line 128. Ridge and the market-column exemption (mve_data lines 304-315) are implemented correctly.

findings.claim: Secondary configuration gap: BOP tops out at c = P/T = 10 whereas DKKM's headline result and their five-characteristic result both use c = 1000 (P=360,000, T=360). With only 5 inputs the RFF Monte-Carlo error at P=3600 is a real constraint on resolving the kernel's small eigenvalues. Also, BOP's shrinkage grid is far heavier than DKKM's optimum.
findings.evidence: config.py N_DKKM_FEATURES_LIST = [6,36,360,3600] and ALPHA_LST = [0,.001,.01,.05,.1,1] (GS21 divides by 100). The applied penalty is 360*nfeatures*alpha added to X'X, and X'X ~ 360*E[ff'], so the effective ridge relative to the mean factor second moment is z_eff = nfeatures*alpha / E[f^2]. At nfeatures=3600, alpha=1e-3, z_eff ~ 3.6/E[f^2] — with unnormalized factor returns E[f^2] is O(1), so z_eff ~ 1-4. DKKM's optimum is z=1e-5 against N^{-1/2}-scaled factors (w33012 footnote 10, section 3.1). The grid essentially never visits the light-shrinkage region. Mitigating evidence that this is secondary: GS21 does explore down to z_eff ~ 0.036 and still prefers alpha=1e-3, i.e. heavy shrinkage genuinely is optimal there — consistent with there being no signal in the extra dimensions.

findings.claim: KP14's negative Sharpes for ALL methods are a separate, diagnosable pathology, and they are the D^{-1} channel operating in isolation and in the wrong direction. Because idiosyncratic return variance is char-linked and extremely dispersed (var proportional to 1/size), the true w* = Sigma^{-1}mu collapses to the inverse-variance tilt (proportional to size), while every empirically estimated tangency portfolio loads on the size premium (proportional to -size). The Sigma-cosine is negative, so the Sharpe is negative, with no sign bug anywhere.
findings.evidence: correlations.csv kp14 rows are all negative (fm -0.0080/-0.148, ff -0.0053/-0.117, dkkm -0.0069/-0.122) while true fitted = 0.568. This is the mechanism already documented in the project memory note docs/kp14_size_idio_var.md. The Sharpe identity SR = SR* * cos_Sigma(w,w*) makes negative Sharpes the necessary consequence of a negative cosine. DKKM 'wins' in KP14 (-0.60 at alpha=1) only by shrinking almost to zero — the least-wrong direction is no direction.

findings.claim: HJD is contaminated by leverage in a way Sharpe is not, and at least one reported HJD is a pure leverage artifact rather than an SDF-accuracy statement.
findings.evidence: create_slides_tables.py lines 49-56 compute HJD = sqrt(mean_t (xret_method,t - sdf_ret_t)^2) on UNNORMALIZED method weights, whereas sdf_ret is the unit-cost-normalized HJ portfolio return (sdf_compute_*.py: port /= port.sum() then sdf_ret = -(port[1:] . (gross ret - gross rf))). Sharpe is scale-invariant, HJD is not. Evidence of the artifact: GS21 FF HJD = 2.3465 while GS21 FF Sharpe = 0.4433 is the best of the three Fama methods; CAPM HJD is 0.4881 and DKKM 0.3300. A 7x HJD with a good Sharpe can only be over-leverage in the OLS tangency weights. Recommendation: report sd(sdf_ret) and the HJD of w=0 as the null, and/or normalize each method's weight to unit predicted cost before computing HJD.

findings.claim: Channel-by-channel: which of the five candidate mechanisms this Sharpe metric can detect. (i) SPAN: fully detectable, it is literally what the Sigma-cosine measures. (ii) DENSITY: detectable, but dimensionally impossible to create with a 17-dimensional effective feature space. (iii) CONDITIONING: detectable, but only BGN's estimator can express it, and only through one channel. (iv) EFFICIENT WEIGHTING (D^{-1}): detectable, but worth 0.19% of SR* at N=1000 unless combined with an unspanned premium. (v) PURE DOUBLE DESCENT: detectable (BOP already see the c=1 spike) but cannot by itself create an advantage — DKKM prove that under correct specification complexity strictly REDUCES the Sharpe ratio.
findings.evidence: (i)-(iv) from span2.py/est3.py as above and the metric identity. (iii): dkkm_functions.rff lines 92-96 rank-standardize the chars and then append rf.values raw for model=='bgn' only, so BGN's index carries a firm-invariant, time-varying phase shift gamma*w_L*rf_t which does rotate the sin/cos features month by month — a genuine conditioning channel. KP14 and GS21 have no time-varying input to the feature map at all, and the ridge coefficient lambda is a single vector estimated on 360 months and applied unchanged to every cross-section (mve_data, estimate_sdf_dkkm.py lines 154-159), so conditioning can only enter through cross-sectionally varying chars. (v): NBER w33012 section 4.6.3: 'The net effect of complexity is an unambiguous decrease in the Sharpe ratio in the correctly specified setting.'

findings.claim: FORMAL STATEMENT of the necessary and sufficient conditions. Write w*_t = Sigma_t^{-1} mu_t, S_t = phi(X_t) in R^{N x P}, F_{t+1} = S_t' R_{t+1}, lambda-hat = (E-hat[FF'] + zI)^{-1} E-hat[F], w-hat_t = S_t lambda-hat. Then Sharpe/SR* = (span ceiling) x (estimation efficiency), where the span ceiling is cos_Sigma(P_{col(S_t)} w*_t, w*_t). Complexity is a virtue iff ALL FIVE of the following hold. (C1) SPAN GAP: the ceiling under the RFF basis materially exceeds the ceiling under the K linear sorts, i.e. g*(x) = w*(x) has large mass orthogonal to the linear-char span in the Sigma inner product. (C2) UNSPANNED PREMIUM: mu_t is NOT of the form B_t lambda_t for a low-rank B_t equal to the dominant covariance loadings; the residual alpha contributes alpha' D^{-1} alpha ~ N * E[alpha^2/d] to SR*^2, growing with N (a near-arbitrage). Without (C2), (C1) is vacuous because the ceiling is 1 for every basis up to O(1/N). (C3) FLAT SPECTRUM: EffRank(E[F F']) = (tr M)^2/tr(M^2) must be in the hundreds (DKKM AIPT alpha=0.5), not single digits (DKKM APT alpha=2.0), AND the risk premia must be aligned with, and spread across, the whole spectrum rather than concentrated in the top 1-2 eigenvectors. (C4) c = P/T must actually be run well above 1 with the shrinkage tuned — the gains are in the c >> 1 region; at c ~ 1 with light shrinkage you get the double-descent collapse. (C5) LIMITS TO LEARNING must bind but not dominate: T must be small enough relative to the true model dimension P* that a correctly-specified small model is infeasible (otherwise the simple model, precisely estimated, wins), and SNR must be high enough that the leading learnable directions are actually learnable (otherwise everything is noise and no ranking emerges). The direct answer to the posed question: if g* is exactly linear in K << P characteristics and SNR is high, theory predicts NO advantage and in fact a strict DISADVANTAGE for ridge-on-P versus OLS-on-K, because the RFF span contains the linear span (so the ceiling is identical) while the estimator pays implicit shrinkage plus complexity risk on the P-K useless directions.
findings.evidence: Metric identity derived above. (C2) magnitudes from span2.py. (C3) is DKKM Theorem 3 parts ii-iii and their Figures 13 vs 14, plus my measured EffRank of 16.5 for the BOP configuration. (C4) is DKKM Figure 2 (P=36 to 360,000, c=0.1 to 1000) and KMZ. (C5) is the DKKM 'implicit shrinkage + complexity risk' decomposition (section 4.6.2) plus the GS21 low-vol counterfactual. The disadvantage claim is verified numerically in est3.py: linear alpha, homogeneous d gives OLS-lin(6)=0.267 vs ridge-RFF(3600)=0.254, and DKKM state the q=1 result analytically.

findings.claim: RANKED LIST of features of real equity cross-sections that create the virtue of complexity and that a 2-shock production model with 5 characteristics lacks — with the structural implementation for each. (1) A non-risk (or non-representative-agent) component of expected returns that is a rich nonlinear function of observable characteristics. Mechanism: limits to arbitrage, sentiment/noise-trader demand, slow-moving capital, intermediary constraints, taxes, index/flow effects. Structural implementation: add a demand or belief wedge delta(x_i,t) to the pricing equation so that E[m R_i] = 1 + delta_i, with delta a smooth but genuinely interactive function of chars and idiosyncratic across firms; OR make the marginal investor segmented so the observed price reflects a different SDF from the one used to compute the true MVE. Note: this changes what 'true' means, so the cleanest version is heterogeneous agents / segmented markets rather than pure mispricing. (2) A high-dimensional priced aggregate risk space. Mechanism: many sectoral, vintage, intangible-capital and financial-constraint shocks, each carrying a price of risk, with heterogeneous char-dependent exposures. Structural implementation: replace the single TFP shock x with a J-dimensional factor structure (J >= 20-50), give each firm a char-dependent loading vector, and let all J be priced. This is the single most direct way to raise EffRank(E[FF']) from ~2 to ~200+. (3) Characteristics as noisy, partial, lagged proxies for the latent states. Mechanism: accounting lags, measurement error, reporting discretion, and the fact that no single characteristic pins down a state. Structural implementation: report x_i,t = h(state) + measurement noise, with several redundant-but-imperfect proxies; also add characteristics that are non-monotone or interactive functions of the states so the map state -> chars is not smoothly invertible. Currently the 5 chars are near-deterministic invertible functions of 2-3 latent states, so w* is a smooth low-order function of them. (4) Characteristic-linked idiosyncratic variance, but ONLY as a multiplier on (1) or (2). Verified: with an unspanned premium present, heteroskedastic D raises the RFF/linear ceiling ratio from 1.53 to 1.91 (linear alpha) and from 2.88 to 6.37 (nonlinear alpha). Without an unspanned premium it is worth 0.2%. (5) Time-varying prices of risk that interact with firm characteristics. Mechanism: countercyclical risk aversion / constraints make the cross-sectional premium of each characteristic move with the macro state. Structural implementation: make beta_i,t depend on x_i,t times a macro state, so that the interaction is visible cross-sectionally; a purely date-level state is invisible to KP14's and GS21's feature maps. (6) A fat left tail of small, high-idiosyncratic-volatility, high-alpha names. DKKM's Sharpe of 3.7 falls to ~1.6 in mega/large caps, so a large part of the real-data VoC is microcap. Structural implementation: a heavier-tailed size distribution and much stronger size-dependence of both alpha and idiosyncratic variance. (7) Non-normality / higher-order priced moments (skewness, jump risk). Minor by comparison.
findings.evidence: Ranking follows from the necessary-condition ordering: (C2) gates everything (span2.py: without alpha, every basis is within 0.6% of SR*), then (C3) EffRank (measured 16.5 vs the required hundreds), then (C1)/span, then the D^{-1} multiplier, then conditioning. Item (6) is from NBER w33012 section 3.6/Figure 9: 'the SDF Sharpe ratios based on mega or large stocks are on the order of 1.6', versus 3.7 full-sample. Item (3) is the reason DKKM's five-characteristic model still works in real data while the models' five characteristics do not.

findings.claim: CHECKLIST + DIAGNOSTICS a structural modeller can run on a simulated panel WITHOUT rerunning the estimator. Five gates, then seven cheap diagnostics. GATES (all must be YES): G1 does the change add expected-return variation NOT spanned by the dominant conditional covariance loadings? G2 is that variation a nonlinear/interactive function of the OBSERVED characteristics (not of latent states the chars do not reveal)? G3 is it spread over MANY quasi-orthogonal directions rather than 1-2 (so that shrinkage-over-many beats selection-over-few)? G4 is the per-direction signal-to-noise such that the leading directions are learnable in T=360 (per-direction Sharpe times sqrt(T) of order 1 or more)? G5 does it raise EffRank(E[F F']) into the hundreds? DIAGNOSTICS: D1 CEILING — mean_t max_sr_t is already stored in every *_moments.pkl; compare to the observed FF/FM/DKKM Sharpes. If FF/SR* is already above ~0.8, no estimator change can help and the DGP must change. This is the single cheapest and most informative number currently not being reported. D2 SPAN GAP (the headline diagnostic, and it IS the maximum attainable DKKM advantage) — per month compute SR_lin,t = sqrt(mu' X (X' Sigma X)^{-1} X' mu) with X = [1, chars] and SR_rff,t = sqrt(mu' S (S' Sigma S)^{-1} S' mu) with S the configured RFF (P=360 suffices); report mean(SR_rff)/mean(SR_lin). Below ~1.5 the model cannot deliver a real-data-sized gap; you want 3-5. The cheaper proxy the task suggested (regress the true w* on linear chars vs a nonlinear basis and compare R^2) is valid ONLY if the regression is Sigma-weighted, because Sharpe is a Sigma-metric cosine; a plain unweighted R^2 on w* is a decent proxy only when Sigma is close to isotropic, which it is not in KP14. D3 PRICING-STRUCTURE RANK — split Sigma_t into common + diagonal, take the top-K eigenvectors of the common part, regress mu_t on them in the D^{-1} metric, and compute the residual alpha_t. Report SR_alpha^2 / SR*^2 = (alpha' D^{-1} alpha)/(mu' Sigma^{-1} mu). If this is below ~0.2 the economy is an APT economy and complexity is provably worthless. This is the gate that all three models currently fail. D4 FACTOR SPECTRUM — form M = time-average of S_t' Sigma_t S_t (or just the sample second moment of the 3600 factor returns you already compute in *_dkkm.pkl) and report EffRank(M) = (tr M)^2/tr(M^2). Target >= 200-500; the feature-side upper bound as configured is 16.5. D5 ALIGNMENT — regress log(squared Sharpe of eigen-portfolio p) on log(eta_p); DKKM's calibration has slope 1.5 with premia spread across the whole spectrum. If all the premium sits in the top 2 PCs, stop. D6 ORACLE COMPLEXITY CURVE — recompute D2's ceiling at P = 36, 360, 3600, 36000. If the ORACLE ceiling is flat in P, the estimated curve will be flat no matter what you do to the ridge. D7 METRIC HYGIENE — report mean_t cos_Sigma(w-hat, w*) alongside Sharpe (it is Sharpe/SR* and is the interpretable number), report sd(sdf_ret) and the HJD of w=0 as the HJD null, and normalize weights to unit predicted cost before computing HJD.
findings.evidence: D1: 'max_sr' is computed and stored in every model's sdf_loop (sdf_compute_bgn.py lines 326-328, sdf_compute_gs21.py lines 222-224, and the KP14 analogue) and saved by calculate_moments.py lines 81-86, but evaluate_sdfs.py never propagates it into results.pkl, so it never reaches the tables. D2/D6 need only rp and cond_var, both already in the moments pickles, plus the S_t you already build. D4 needs only the factor returns already stored in *_dkkm.pkl. The Sigma-weighting caveat in D2 follows directly from the Sharpe = SR* x cos_Sigma identity. Validation that D2 is the right ceiling: in span2.py the oracle ratio RFF/lin (0.994 under exact FP, 21 under nonlinear alpha + het d) correctly ordered the estimated outcomes in est3.py (0.093/0.058 flat, versus 1.249/0.110 with a rising VoC curve).

verdict_on_hypotheses.hypothesis: H1 SPAN — with only 1-2 priced aggregate shocks and 5-6 chars that are near-deterministic functions of 2-3 latent states, the true conditional MVE is already (over-)spanned by 6 linear characteristic portfolios, so complexity has nothing to buy.
verdict_on_hypotheses.reasoning: Confirmed, and the mechanism is stronger and simpler than stated. It is not merely that 6 linear portfolios happen to span the MVE; it is that under exact K-factor pricing with N=1000, ANY well-diversified portfolio with the right factor exposure attains the maximum Sharpe to within 0.19% (measured: SR*=0.0999 vs equal-weight 0.0998 vs linear span 0.0999 vs RFF 0.0994; span2.py). The models are frictionless rational-expectations economies in which mu is by construction minus the covariance with m, and the number of aggregate shocks is 1 (GS21) or 2 (BGN, KP14). So the span ceiling for the RFF basis relative to the FF/FM basis is 1.00, and no estimator improvement can move it.

verdict_on_hypotheses.hypothesis: H2 RATIO NONLINEARITY — with Sigma = B Omega B' + D, w* = D^{-1} B c is a ratio b(x)/d(x), nonlinear even when b and d are each linear; FF sorts and FM's (X'X)^{-1}X' cannot form it; currently d_i may be too homogeneous or too weakly char-linked.
verdict_on_hypotheses.reasoning: The algebra is right but the channel is conditionally worthless. Under exact factor pricing the D^{-1} tilt is worth 1/(2 sigma_f^2 beta'D^{-1}beta) of the maximum Sharpe, which I measured at 1.81% (N=100), 0.186% (N=1000), 0.019% (N=10000) — and it is worth essentially nothing EVEN WITH extreme d dispersion (d spanning a 20x range: SR*=0.1000, linear span=0.1000). The reason: idiosyncratic risk is diversifiable, so the inverse-variance tilt only buys back the un-diversified residual, which is O(1/N). Heteroskedastic D becomes powerful only as a MULTIPLIER on an unspanned premium: with a linear alpha present it raises the RFF/linear ceiling ratio from 1.00 to 1.91 and cuts the linear span's share of SR* from 1.00 to 0.31; with a nonlinear alpha it raises it from 2.88 to 6.37. So: making d more char-linked is a good second-order move but is a dead end on its own. KP14 is the cautionary case — its d dispersion is already extreme (var proportional to 1/size) and it produces large NEGATIVE Sharpes.

verdict_on_hypotheses.hypothesis: H3 RFF BANDWIDTH MIS-SCALING — with L=5 rank-standardized chars, sd(w'x) <= 0.65, sin is essentially linear over that range, the basis is approximately {linear index, quadratic index}, and gamma should be rescaled by sqrt(130/L).
verdict_on_hypotheses.reasoning: The descriptive claim is confirmed with precision: measured sd(w'x) = 0.526 (L=5) and 0.580 (L=6), 99th percentile |z| = 1.55; the mean RFF feature has R^2 = 0.860 on a degree-2 polynomial in the 5 chars and only 0.878 on degree 3; the participation-ratio effective rank of the whole 3600-feature map is 16.5. Rescaling works as predicted: gamma x8 lifts effective rank to 379 (c ~ 1.05) and gamma x12 to 661. BUT the proposed fix is NOT the answer and can backfire. (a) DKKM use the IDENTICAL gamma grid [0.5..1.0] and the identical [-0.5,0.5] rank-standardization, and their five-characteristic model still delivers 0.74 -> 1.93-2.50 in real data — so the bandwidth is not what separates the two settings. (b) In my estimation experiment the x8 bandwidth HURT badly whenever the truth was low-order (linear alpha, homogeneous d: 0.157 vs 0.254 for the config bandwidth) and helped only when the truth had genuine high-frequency content (nonlinear alpha, homogeneous d: 0.665 vs 0.630). Widening the bandwidth adds reachable dimensions but spreads a fixed P over them more thinly. Treat it as a robustness knob, not a fix.

verdict_on_hypotheses.hypothesis: H4 CHARACTERISTIC POVERTY — real DKKM uses ~130 chars with many weak partly-independent signals; here there are 5-6, mutually redundant and noiselessly measured; the theory requires the truth to be dense and high-dimensional in feature space.
verdict_on_hypotheses.reasoning: The mechanical part is confirmed and quantified: with the config gamma, the RFF effective rank goes 16.5 (L=5), 20.7 (6), 38.5 (10), 98.3 (20), 432 (50), 773 (130). L=130 lands you squarely in DKKM's AIPT regime (their calibrated EffRank ~ 500) and L=5 lands you in their APT regime (EffRank ~ 2.5), which is exactly the observed behaviour. BUT the hypothesis is REFUTED as the fundamental cause, by DKKM's own five-characteristic experiment: with only size, value, investment, profitability and momentum — the same five BOP use — real data still yields FF6 = 0.74 -> complex = 1.93-2.50 (2.6-3.4x). Five characteristics are enough in real data because the true SDF weight is a strongly nonlinear function of them; in these models it is not, or the nonlinear part is unlearnable. Adding characteristics to the models will not help unless the added characteristics carry genuinely new, nonlinearly-priced information. The 'noiselessly measured, mutually redundant' clause is the part that matters most: chars that are smooth invertible functions of 2-3 latent states cannot support a dense signal.

verdict_on_hypotheses.hypothesis: H5 HJD SCALE MISMATCH — sdf_ret and the method returns w.xret have different and possibly wildly different scales; if sd(sdf_ret) >> sd(xret_method) then HJD ~ sd(sdf_ret) for every method and the metric cannot separate them.
verdict_on_hypotheses.reasoning: Confirmed that HJD is scale-sensitive (unlike Sharpe, which is exactly scale-invariant) and that at least one reported HJD is a leverage artifact: GS21's FF HJD is 2.3465 while GS21's FF Sharpe (0.4433) is the best of the three Fama methods, and CAPM's HJD is 0.4881 — a 5-7x HJD with a good Sharpe can only be over-leverage in the unpenalized OLS tangency weights. NOT confirmed in the direction stated: the BGN HJDs (CAPM 0.296, FF 0.218, FM 0.223, DKKM 0.201) do separate the methods and move in the same order as Sharpe, so the metric is not structurally saturated there. I could not verify sd(sdf_ret) because no *_results.pkl or *_moments.pkl files are present in this checkout (outputs/ is empty). Recommendation: report sd(sdf_ret) and the HJD of w=0 as the null, and normalize each method's weights to unit predicted cost before differencing.

verdict_on_hypotheses.hypothesis: H6 EVALUATION HORIZON / SNR — if the model panels have far higher cross-sectional predictability than real data (~0.5%/month), estimation is easy, OLS on 6 factors is efficient, and the ridge advantage never appears.
verdict_on_hypotheses.reasoning: Refuted as stated — the sign is backwards. Estimation is not easy here, it is impossible: the mean cross-sectional correlation between each method's stock weight and the true SDF weight is 0.0000-0.0058 in absolute value for FF, FM AND DKKM across all three models (correlations.csv), with a cross-month sd of ~0.033, i.e. all three estimators are statistically indistinguishable from noise at the stock level. The GS21 low-volatility run is the controlled counterfactual: raising SNR lifts corr(method, truth) to 0.746-0.803 for all three and — importantly — makes DKKM the BEST method (0.803 vs ff 0.771 vs fm 0.746). So the correct restatement is: SNR is too LOW, raising it is NECESSARY for any method to recover anything, and it flips the ranking to the right order — but it delivers only a ~4% DKKM edge, not the 3-5x seen in real data. Raising SNR alone will not produce the target result.

quantitative_claims: METRIC IDENTITY (exact): Sharpe_t(w) = SR*_t x cos_{Sigma_t}(w, w*_t) with w* = Sigma^{-1} rp and SR*_t = sqrt(rp' Sigma^{-1} rp) = the already-computed `max_sr`. Scale-invariant in w; can be negative.

TARGET TO MATCH REAL DATA: DKKM/FF Sharpe ratio of 3-5x (currently 1.04 for BGN, 1.15 for GS21), DKKM HJD at ~0.5x the benchmark HJD (currently 0.92x for BGN), and a monotonically rising VoC curve over c from 0.1 to 1000 (currently flat at +2.5%).
blockers: 1. NO UNSPANNED PREMIUM (the binding constraint). All three models impose exact low-K factor pricing: mu_t is, by construction, minus the conditional covariance of returns with the model's own SDF, and there are only 1 (GS21) or 2 (BGN, KP14) aggregate shocks. Under exact K-factor pricing with N=1000, the maximum conditional Sharpe is attained to within 0.19% by ANY well-diversified portfolio with the right factor exposure (measured: SR*=0.0999 vs equal-weight 0.0998 vs 6 linear char portfolios 0.0999 vs the full 3600-feature RFF 0.0994). The RFF-over-linear span ceiling is therefore 1.00. No estimator, shrinkage level, bandwidth or feature count can create an advantage that does not exist in the population. What is missing is a component of expected returns that is NOT proportional to the dominant conditional covariance loadings and whose contribution to SR*^2 is alpha' D^{-1} alpha ~ N x E[alpha^2/d], i.e. that grows with N — the AIPT near-arbitrage. Economically: segmented/heterogeneous marginal investors, demand or belief wedges, limits to arbitrage, or intermediary constraints.

2. PRICED-RISK SPACE IS ONE- OR TWO-DIMENSIONAL, SO THE MANAGED-PORTFOLIO SPECTRUM IS DEGENERATE. DKKM's Theorem 3 makes the criterion explicit and it is a criterion on EffRank(E[F F']) = (tr M)^2/tr(M^2): their AIPT calibration (eta_p ~ p^{-0.5}, EffRank ~ 500) produces the virtue of complexity, their APT calibration (eta_p ~ p^{-2}, EffRank ~ 2.5) produces none and makes complexity harmful at light shrinkage, with peak performance at c << 1. The BOP results are a line-for-line reproduction of the APT calibration, including the harm at alpha=0 (GS21 goes 0.498 -> 0.034 -> 0.177 as P rises) and the peak at heavy shrinkage. The fix is to raise the number of independently priced aggregate shocks with heterogeneous, characteristic-dependent loadings — from 1-2 to tens.

3. THE FEATURE MAP IS ONLY ~17-DIMENSIONAL, SO THE P/T ASYMPTOTICS NEVER ENGAGE. Measured effective rank of the 3600-feature RFF map as configured: 16.50 (5 chars) / 20.71 (6 chars). Nominal c = 10; effective c = 0.046. The average feature is 86% a quadratic polynomial in the five characteristics (degree 3 adds only 1.8 points of R^2), because sd(w'x) = 0.53 confines sin/cos to their near-linear range. Even if the DGP were fixed, the estimator as configured would only be able to express roughly 'FM plus pairwise interactions'. Two levers: raise the input dimension (measured EffRank 16.5 at L=5, 98 at L=20, 773 at L=130), or widen gamma (x8 gives EffRank 379) — but the second lever is double-edged and hurt badly in my estimation experiment whenever the truth was low-order.

4. THE FIVE CHARACTERISTICS ARE NOISELESS, REDUNDANT, SMOOTH, INVERTIBLE FUNCTIONS OF 2-3 LATENT STATES. This is why the true SDF weight is a low-order function of them and why the nonlinear part is small. Note the counterexample that disciplines this blocker: DKKM get a 2.6-3.4x complexity gain in REAL data using exactly these same five characteristics, so the problem is not the count but the informational structure. What is missing is measurement error, reporting lags, and characteristics that are non-monotone or interactive proxies for the states, so that recovering w*(x) actually requires a rich function class.

5. SIGNAL-TO-NOISE IS SO LOW THAT ALL THREE ESTIMATORS ARE NOISE, SO NO RANKING CAN EMERGE. corr(method weight, true weight) is 0.0000-0.0058 in absolute value for FF, FM and DKKM in all three models, against a cross-month sd of 0.033. The GS21 low-volatility run is the clean counterfactual: it lifts all three to 0.746-0.803 and makes DKKM the best (0.803 vs FF 0.771 vs FM 0.746). So raising SNR is a necessary precondition for any comparison to mean anything — but on its own it buys only a ~4% DKKM edge, not the 3-5x target. Fix this second, after blockers 1-3.

6. NO CONDITIONING CHANNEL IN THE ESTIMATOR FOR KP14 AND GS21. The ridge coefficient lambda is a single vector estimated on 360 months and applied unchanged to every cross-section, so time-varying prices of risk can only be captured through cross-sectionally varying inputs. BGN alone has one: rf_stand is appended raw (not rank-standardized) in dkkm_functions.rff, giving a time-varying phase shift of the sin/cos index. KP14 and GS21 have no time-varying input at all. Any conditioning story added to those models must show up as a characteristic x macro-state INTERACTION visible in the cross-section, not as a date-level state.

7. c = P/T TOPS OUT AT 10 WHILE THE PUBLISHED RESULT NEEDS c = 1000, AND THE SHRINKAGE GRID NEVER VISITS THE LIGHT-PENALTY REGION. N_DKKM_FEATURES_LIST maxes at 3600 (c=10); DKKM's headline and their five-characteristic result both use P=360,000 (c=1000). BOP's effective ridge at the smallest nonzero grid point with 3600 features is z_eff ~ O(1-4) relative to the mean factor second moment, versus DKKM's optimum of 1e-5. This is a cheap thing to fix and worth ruling out, but I rank it last: GS21 already explores down to z_eff ~ 0.036 and still prefers heavy shrinkage, which is exactly what you expect when there is no signal in the extra dimensions.

8. MEASUREMENT HYGIENE THAT IS CURRENTLY HIDING THE ANSWER. The single most informative number — mean_t max_sr_t, the true maximum conditional Sharpe — is already computed in every sdf_loop and saved into *_moments.pkl, but evaluate_sdfs.py never propagates it into results.pkl, so it never reaches a table. Without it nobody can tell whether FF at 0.2423 is 10% or 90% of the ceiling, which is the difference between 'the estimator is failing' and 'the model has nothing to estimate'. Relatedly, HJD is computed on unnormalized weights and is contaminated by leverage (GS21 FF HJD = 2.3465 alongside the best Fama Sharpe of 0.4433), and Sharpe should be reported as Sharpe/SR* = the Sigma-metric cosine, which is the interpretable quantity.
